Title of the Talk: Talk 1 : Tiny Shells, Deep Time: How Marine Carbonates Record Earth’s Climate
Speaker Name: Sambuddha Mishra — Associate Professor, Centre for Earth Sciences, Indian Institute of Science- Bangalore
Abstract: Earth’s long-term climate stability is maintained by a delicate balance between the release of greenhouse gases from Earth’s interior and their removal through the chemical weathering of rocks. As continental rocks weather, they consume atmospheric CO₂ and deliver dissolved elements to the oceans, thereby regulating both climate and seawater chemistry. Marine organisms incorporate these chemical signatures into their calcium carbonate shells, preserving an archive of past ocean conditions over millions of years. My research uses trace elements and boron isotopes preserved in microscopic marine fossils called foraminifera to reconstruct the evolution of Earth’s climate and ocean chemistry through time. In this talk, I will discuss how, and why, marine carbonates remain among the most faithful natural archives of past climate change.
Profile of the Speaker: Sambuddha Misra is an Associate Professor at the Centre for Earth Sciences, Indian Institute of Science. He obtained his B.Sc. and M.Sc. from the University of Calcutta, followed by a PhD in Chemical Oceanography from the Florida State University. He subsequently held postdoctoral and research positions at the University of Cambridge before joining IISc in 2017. His research investigates the role of silicate weathering and reverse weathering in regulating Earth’s long-term climate and develops isotope-based approaches to trace the sources and pathways of environmental pollution. He also develops geochemical proxies to reconstruct past ocean chemistry and climate from marine and terrestrial archives. His research combines non-traditional stable isotopes, radiogenic isotopes, and trace element geochemistry to address fundamental questions in Earth system science. He serves as Associate Editor of Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta and leads a research group of PhD students and postdoctoral fellows at IISc.

Title of the Talk: Talk 2: How Mangroves Lock Away Carbon—and Why It Matters
Speaker Name: Indra Sekhar Sen, Associate Professor, Department of Earth Sciences, Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur
Abstract:
Mangrove forests do much more than protect coastlines—they are also among the world's most powerful natural carbon stores. Hidden beneath their muddy soils lies a vast reserve of carbon that has been locked away for hundreds to thousands of years, helping to slow climate change. But what happens when these forests are damaged? Can restoring them recover their ability to store carbon and help fight climate change? 

In this talk, I will show how tiny geochemical clues preserved in mangrove soils reveal how these remarkable ecosystems capture and store carbon over centuries. Using examples from the Sundarbans, I will explain how scientists trace the journey of carbon—from where it comes from to how long it remains stored—and why this matters in the fight against climate change.
Profile of the Speaker: Dr. Indra Sekhar Sen is an isotope geochemist and Associate Professor in the Department of Earth Sciences at the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur (IIT Kanpur). He earned his Ph.D. from Florida International University, USA, in 2010 and completed postdoctoral research at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI), USA, from 2010 to 2013. His research spans environmental geochemistry, carbon cycling, water quality, and climate change. He currently serves as Associate Editor for Global and Planetary Change (Elsevier), Geophysical Research Letters (American Geophysical Union), and the Vadose Zone Journal (Soil Science Society of America).

Title of the Talk: Talk 4: Carbon, Commodity, Community: the Science and Practice of Nature-based Solutions
Speaker Name: Ghazala Shahabuddin, Visiting Faculty of Environmental Studies, Ashoka University
Abstract: Globally, nature-based solutions (NBS), involving conservation and restoration of natural ecosystems, have considerable potential for mitigating climate change. Recent advances in ecological sciences have indicated that NBS could have sizeable, sustainable and positive impacts on carbon sequestration rates. In addition NBS could potentially ameliorate some of the adverse spin-offs of warming on agriculture, forestry and other economic activity. However, such positive impacts of NBS are dependent on the judicious incorporation of both scientific and social goals as well as the quality of implementation. In many cases, the positive goals of NBS are being subverted by a reductionist approach to ecosystem conservation and restoration, which relies on extreme forms of commodification. The speaker will first describe the potential of NBS based on scientific evidence from forests, grasslands and wetlands. She will then go into the possible pitfalls of NBS, particularly as exhibited in the context of Indian society.
Profile of the Speaker: Ghazala Shahabuddin has a PhD in Ecology and Conservation Biology from Duke University, USA (1998) for which she studied the ecological impacts of habitat fragmentation in Lago Guri, Venezuela. Her research has since expanded to include larger social-ecological issues at the interface of human society and biodiversity, including biodiversity governance and land use change impacts. She has carried out pioneering field studies on forest birds in the Himalayas, Aravalli Hills and in Rajasthan. She has published extensively in the area of wildlife policy and politics in India. Her book ‘Conservation at the Crossroads’ (Permanent Black, 2010) critically examines contemporary wildlife policy and implementation in India. She was Associate Professor at Dr. B.R. Ambedkar University in Delhi where she helped develop the University’s flagship Master’s programme in Environment and Development (2009-14). She is currently a Visiting Professor at Ashoka University, India, and carried out field research on long-term ecological changes in Himalayan forests and their interface with local communities in Uttarakhand.

Title of the Talk: Talk 5: Climate change & Infectious disease Modelling
Speaker Name: Gautam Menon, Professor of Physics and Biology, Ashoka University
Profile of the Speaker:
Gautam Menon is a Professor of Physics and Biology at Ashoka University.
He served as Dean (Research) at Ashoka between 2022 and 2025 and was also Director of Ashoka’s Centre for Climate Change and Sustainability (3CS) during that period.
He is a Commissioner on the Lancet Commission on “Strengthening the use of Epidemiological Modelling of Pandemic Diseases”, a co-author of the “Lancet Commission on a Citizen-centred Health System for India” and a member of the WHO “Technical Advisory Group on Embedding Ethics in Health and Climate Change Policy.” He completed a BSc (Hons) in physics at St. Stephen’s College, Delhi, an MSc from IIT Kanpur, and a PhD from the Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore. Prior to joining Ashoka, he was a Professor with both the Theoretical Physics and Computational Biology groups at the Institute of Mathematical Sciences (IMSc), Chennai, where he was also the founding Dean of the Computational Biology group. He joined IMSc following post-doctoral research and teaching at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research in Mumbai and the Simon Fraser University in Vancouver, Canada. He was a Visiting Professor at the Mechanobiology Institute and the Department of Biological Sciences at the National University of Singapore (2011 – 2013). He was an Adjunct Professor at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, Mumbai (2019 – 2022). He serves on the scientific review committees of several international and national agencies, including the Human Frontier Science Program and the Wellcome Trust-DBT India Alliance, as well as on a number of national committees. He was a Member of the Expert Group (Education) for the Science, Technology and Innovation Policy of India (2020).

Title of the Talk: Talk 6: More participation, less AI: Lessons from the CoRE stack - a digital public infrastructure for climate change adaptation of rural communities
Speaker Name: Aaditeshwar Seth, Professor, Department of Computer Science and Engineering- Indian Institute of Technology- Delhi
Abstract: The CoRE Stack (Commoning for Resilience and Equality) is a community-based digital public infrastructure consisting of datasets, algorithm pipelines, and user-facing tools, that can be used by rural communities and other stakeholders to improve the sustainability and resilience of their local landscapes. It is hoped that data-driven reasoning will help design appropriate interventions for water security, forest restoration, grassland health, and improved biodiversity, while being in harmony with fulfilling social and economic aspirations of the communities. At the same time, data can have errors and not everything might be observed in the data; community involvement and ownership is critical, and I will present the experience of numerous CoRE stack partners with successfully finding a sweet spot between using data but without compromising on community participation.
Profile of the Speaker: Aaditeshwar Seth is a professor in the Department of Computer Science and Engineering at the Indian Institute of Technology Delhi, and co-founder of the social technology enterprise Gram Vaani and of the CoRE stack infrastructure and network. He is passionate about building appropriate technologies and participatory tools that can empower marginalized communities to collectivize and voice themselves, and especially to build climate resilience. Several million people, and over 200 organizations worldwide, have directly touched technology platforms built by Aaditeshwar’s team at Gram Vaani, the CoRE stack, and his students at the ACT4D (Appropriate Computing Technologies for Development) research group at IIT Delhi. Many elements of their work have also been adopted by government departments and have influenced the use of technologies for development in the social sector. He is a recipient of the ACM SIGCHI Social Impact Award for 2022. His book published in 2022, Technology and (Dis)Empowerment: A Call to Technologists, argues that the primary goal of technologists should be to bring equality and overturn unjust social and economic structures through their inventions.

Title of the Talk: Introductory remarks on the Policy and Governance architecture for Climate Policy and Climate Negotiations
Speaker Name: Dr Krishna Gupta, IAS, Additional Chief Secretary, Department of Mass Extension Education and Library Services and Department of Cooperation and Dr Imroze Khan, Director, Centre for Climate Change & Sustainability (3CS)
Uday Shankar, Professor and Dean, Rajiv Gandhi School of Intellectual Property Law, Indian Institute of Technology- Kharagpur
Sumedha Basu, Assistant Professor, Environmental Studies, Ashoka University
Profile of the Speaker:
Sumedha Basu is an Assistant Professor of Environmental Studies at Ashoka University. Before joining Ashoka, she held a postdoctoral position at the Sustainability Research Institute at the University of Leeds, where she also served as Research Co-lead of the Energy and Climate Change Mitigation Research Cluster. At Leeds, she contributed to a UK Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC)–funded programme on urban energy transitions and led two independent research projects supported by the Leeds Social Sciences Institute and the Horizon Institute. Sumedha holds a PhD in Politics and International Studies from the University of Warwick (UK) and an MSc in Environmental Studies from TERI University, New Delhi. Between 2014 and 2016, she was awarded fellowships by the Technical University of Dresden and the Alexander von Humboldt Foundation, Germany. As part of the latter, she was affiliated with the Wuppertal Institute for Climate, Environment, and Energy.

Sumedha’s research interests lie at the intersection of societal implications of sustainable energy transitions and climate action and the concomitant institutional responses. Through her interdisciplinary research, Sumedha is particularly keen to foreground politics, justice, and democratic dimensions in climate and energy transition governance in South Asia. In her doctoral research, she brought together political power, multilevel governance, and socio-technical transitions scholarship to elucidate how cities are shaping and are being shaped by India’s evolving energy transition landscape. She is also interested in exploring alternative conceptual frameworks and research methodologies to address global environmental challenges that would imminently demand society-wide systemic transformations. She has developed a complex systems–based framework for planning sustainable urban energy transitions, which she applied to the study of sustainable cooling pathways in an Indian city during her postdoctoral research. More recently, she has extended this work to examine the interlinkages between urban informality and climate risk through co-produced, participatory research methodologies.

Sumedha has taught courses on climate change and sustainability at multiple universities, including Warwick, Leeds, Oxford, and Nottingham Trent University. She is passionate about teaching that connects theory with real-world challenges and encourages students to think critically about climate solutions. Drawing on over a decade of experience in policy advisory and development work across South Asia, she brings practical insights from renewable energy, climate finance, energy access, and urban sustainability fields into the classroom. Beyond teaching and research, Sumedha actively engages with government agencies, civil society organisations, and international institutions, and encourages students to explore how academic knowledge can inform policy and social change.
